claim: E1 and E2 (E1E2), the fusion proteins of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), are unlike that of any other virus yet described.
source: E1 and E2 (E1E2), the fusion proteins of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), are unlike that of any other virus yet described, and the detailed molecular mechanisms of HCV entry/fusion remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Hypervariable region-1 (HVR-1) of E2 is a putative intrinsically disordered protein tail.
source: Hypervariable region-1 (HVR-1) of E2 is a putative intrinsically disordered protein tail.
evidence: This statement is based on prior characterization and is referenced in the manuscript's introduction and results sections.

claim: HVR-1 has an autoinhibitory function that suppresses the activity of E1E2 on free virions.
source: Here, we demonstrate that HVR-1 has an autoinhibitory function that suppresses the activity of E1E2 on free virions; this is dependent on its conformational entropy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including MD simulations, biophysical analysis, and functional assays.

claim: The autoinhibitory function of HVR-1 is dependent on its conformational entropy.
source: Here, we demonstrate that HVR-1 has an autoinhibitory function that suppresses the activity of E1E2 on free virions; this is dependent on its conformational entropy.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulations showing HVR-1 dynamics and biophysical measurements of disorder.

claim: The HVR-1 autoinhibitory mechanism is turned off by host receptor interactions at the cell surface to allow entry.
source: Crucially, this mechanism is turned off by host receptor interactions at the cell surface to allow entry.
evidence: This is supported by receptor dependency experiments and mathematical modeling showing SR-B1's role in priming entry.

claim: Mutations that reduce conformational entropy in HVR-1 turn off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV.
source: Mutations that reduce conformational entropy in HVR-1, or genetic deletion of HVR-1, turn off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV that exhibits enhanced virus entry but is thermally unstable and acutely sensitive to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with I438V A524T and other mutants showing increased infectivity, decreased stability, and increased antibody sensitivity.

claim: Genetic deletion of HVR-1 turns off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV.
source: Mutations that reduce conformational entropy in HVR-1, or genetic deletion of HVR-1, turn off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV that exhibits enhanced virus entry but is thermally unstable and acutely sensitive to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with ΔHVR-1 virus showing hyper-reactive phenotype.

claim: Hyper-reactive HCV exhibits enhanced virus entry.
source: Mutations that reduce conformational entropy in HVR-1, or genetic deletion of HVR-1, turn off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV that exhibits enhanced virus entry but is thermally unstable and acutely sensitive to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is shown by infectivity assays and entry kinetics measurements.

claim: Hyper-reactive HCV is thermally unstable.
source: Mutations that reduce conformational entropy in HVR-1, or genetic deletion of HVR-1, turn off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV that exhibits enhanced virus entry but is thermally unstable and acutely sensitive to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by thermal stability assays at 37°C showing decreased half-life.

claim: Hyper-reactive HCV is acutely sensitive to neutralising antibodies.
source: Mutations that reduce conformational entropy in HVR-1, or genetic deletion of HVR-1, turn off the safety catch to generate hyper-reactive HCV that exhibits enhanced virus entry but is thermally unstable and acutely sensitive to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is shown by neutralization assays with patient IgG and monoclonal antibodies.

claim: The HVR-1 safety catch controls the efficiency of virus entry.
source: Therefore, the HVR-1 safety catch controls the efficiency of virus entry and maintains resistance to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by infectivity measurements and mathematical modeling of entry efficiency.

claim: The HVR-1 safety catch maintains resistance to neutralising antibodies.
source: Therefore, the HVR-1 safety catch controls the efficiency of virus entry and maintains resistance to neutralising antibodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neutralization experiments and antibody selection experiments.

claim: HCV entry involves at least four host factors: CD81, scavenger receptor B-1 (SR-B1), claudin-1 and occludin.
source: HCV entry involves at least four host factors: CD81, scavenger receptor B-1 (SR-B1), claudin-1 and occludin.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Epidermal growth factor receptor signalling contributes to receptor-complex formation and particle endocytosis.
source: Additionally, epidermal growth factor receptor signalling contributes to receptor-complex formation and particle endocytosis, followed by endosomal, pH-dependent, fusion (Baktash et al., 2018; Evans et al., 2007; Lupberger et al., 2011; Pileri et al., 1998; Ploss et al., 2009; Scarselli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HCV entry is followed by endosomal, pH-dependent, fusion.
source: Additionally, epidermal growth factor receptor signalling contributes to receptor-complex formation and particle endocytosis, followed by endosomal, pH-dependent, fusion (Baktash et al., 2018; Evans et al., 2007; Lupberger et al., 2011; Pileri et al., 1998; Ploss et al., 2009; Scarselli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only SR-B1 and CD81 interact directly with HCV.
source: Current evidence indicates that only SR-B1 and CD81 interact directly with HCV, via the major glycoprotein E2, and that the minor glycoprotein, E1, contains the fusogen (Hu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020; Perin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SR-B1 and CD81 interact with HCV via the major glycoprotein E2.
source: Current evidence indicates that only SR-B1 and CD81 interact directly with HCV, via the major glycoprotein E2, and that the minor glycoprotein, E1, contains the fusogen (Hu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020; Perin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The minor glycoprotein E1 contains the fusogen.
source: Current evidence indicates that only SR-B1 and CD81 interact directly with HCV, via the major glycoprotein E2, and that the minor glycoprotein, E1, contains the fusogen (Hu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020; Perin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: By day 42 of continuous culture, substitutions were detected throughout the HCV genome.
source: By day 42 we detected substitutions throughout the genome (before this, no mutations reached >5% frequency).
evidence: This is based on NGS data from the evolution experiment.

claim: The viral entry glycoproteins E1E2 were particularly enriched for non-synonymous substitutions when compared to other coding regions.
source: The viral entry glycoproteins, E1E2, were particularly enriched for non-synonymous substitutions when compared to other coding regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting adaptive optimisation of virus entry.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NGS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The enrichment of non-synonymous substitutions in E1E2 suggests adaptive optimisation of virus entry.
source: The viral entry glycoproteins, E1E2, were particularly enriched for non-synonymous substitutions when compared to other coding regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting adaptive optimisation of virus entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed mutation pattern.

claim: Introduction of I438V and A524T mutations by reverse genetics resulted in a stepwise increase in HCV infectivity.
source: Introduction of these sequential mutations, by reverse genetics, resulted in a stepwise increase in HCV infectivity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by infectivity assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: WT and mutant viruses were equally dependent on CD81, CLDN1, and OCLN.
source: WT and mutant viruses were equally dependent on CD81, CLDN1, and OCLN, whereas the requirement for SR-B1 decreased in the mutant viruses in a manner that mirrored viral titre.
evidence: This is shown by receptor knockout experiments in Figure 1B.

claim: The requirement for SR-B1 decreased in the mutant viruses in a manner that mirrored viral titre.
source: WT and mutant viruses were equally dependent on CD81, CLDN1, and OCLN, whereas the requirement for SR-B1 decreased in the mutant viruses in a manner that mirrored viral titre.
evidence: This is shown by receptor knockout experiments in Figure 1B.

claim: The efficiency of HCV entry is tightly linked to SR-B1 dependency.
source: This demonstrates that the efficiency of HCV entry is tightly linked to SR-B1 dependency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between infectivity and SR-B1 dependency.

claim: I438V A524T HCV was largely resistant to inhibition by anti-SR-B1.
source: CD81 blockade prevented entry of both viruses equally - consistent with CD81 being an essential receptor - whereas the I438V A524T mutant was largely resistant to inhibition by anti-SR-B1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody blockade experiments in Figure 1C.

claim: I438V A524T sE2 exhibited >2 fold reduction in SR-B1 binding.
source: I438V A524T sE2 exhibited altered receptor interactions, with >2 fold reduction in SR-B1 binding and >2 fold increase in CD81 interaction.
evidence: This is shown by sE2 binding assays in Figure 1E & F.

claim: I438V A524T sE2 exhibited >2 fold increase in CD81 interaction.
source: I438V A524T sE2 exhibited altered receptor interactions, with >2 fold reduction in SR-B1 binding and >2 fold increase in CD81 interaction.
evidence: This is shown by sE2 binding assays in Figure 1E & F.

claim: I438V A524T HCV was >3 fold less stable than WT virus at 37°C.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that I438V A524T HCV was >3 fold less stable than WT virus (assessed by comparison of half-life, Figure 2A); this would suggest that the I438V A524T mutations increase the propensity for E1E2 to undergo spontaneous inactivation, such that particles become non-infectious more rapidly than WT; this is reminiscent of a hyper-reactive state observed in HIV-1 Env and a related phenotype in West Nile Virus (Goo et al., 2017; Haim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by thermal stability assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: I438V A524T HCV completes entry ~3 times faster than WT.
source: Comparison of time to 50% entry suggests that I438V A524T HCVcc completes entry ~3 times faster than WT.
evidence: This is predicted by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 2C and confirmed experimentally in Figure 2D.

claim: WT HCV was highly resistant to patient nAbs.
source: WT HCV was highly resistant to patient nAbs (Figure 3A); the neutralisation curve followed a log-linear relationship, such that successive 10-fold increases in IgG concentration yielded only a modest increase in neutralisation.
evidence: This is shown by neutralization assays in Figure 3A.

claim: I438V A524T mutant was acutely sensitive to patient IgG, reaching complete neutralisation even at low concentrations.
source: In contrast, the hyper-reactive I438V A524T mutant was acutely sensitive to IgG, reaching complete neutralisation even at low concentrations.
evidence: This is shown by neutralization assays in Figure 3A.

claim: Without exception, WT virus resisted neutralisation whereas I438V A524T HCV was potently inhibited by a panel of mAbs.
source: Without exception, WT virus resisted neutralisation whereas I438V A524T HCV was potently inhibited; this is best illustrated by examining the change in IC50 values across the panel, which demonstrates a~20-fold increase in sensitivity to mAbs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neutralization assays with multiple mAbs shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: There is a ~20-fold increase in sensitivity to mAbs for I438V A524T HCV compared to WT.
source: Without exception, WT virus resisted neutralisation whereas I438V A524T HCV was potently inhibited; this is best illustrated by examining the change in IC50 values across the panel, which demonstrates a~20-fold increase in sensitivity to mAbs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by IC50 measurements in Figure 3D.

claim: mAbs bound equally to WT and I438V A524T E2.
source: Without exception, mAbs bound equally to WT and I438V A524T E2, suggesting that WT and mutant E2 are antigenically equivalent.
evidence: This is shown by ELISA binding assays in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: I438V A524T hyper-reactivity was preserved on HCVpp.
source: Nonetheless, I438V A524T hyper-reactivity (low SR-B1 dependency, instability and nAb sensitivity) was preserved on HCVpp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which do not exhibit lipoprotein associations (Hsu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with HCVpp shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hyper-reactive phenotype is intrinsic to E1E2 and does not require contribution from host lipoproteins components.
source: Therefore, the hyper-reactive phenotype is intrinsic to E1E2 and does not require contribution from host lipoproteins components.
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation of hyper-reactivity in HCVpp which lack lipoprotein associations.

claim: Both WT and I438V A524T pseudoparticles were resistant to acid treatment.
source: Both WT and I438V A524T pseudoparticles were resistant to acid treatment, whereas control pseudoparticles bearing Chikungunya E1E2 were potently inactivated (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is shown by pH sensitivity assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: I438V A524T displayed a CD81-dependent sensitivity to treatment at both pH 6 and 5.
source: Here, WT pseudoparticles remained acid-resistant, whereas I438V A524T displayed a CD81-dependent sensitivity to treatment at both pH 6 and 5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown by pH sensitivity assays with sCD81 in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The HVR-1 tail of I438V A524T E2 exhibited consistent stabilisation.
source: However, the HVR-1 tail of I438V A524T E2 exhibited consistent stabilisation (Figure 4), this is best illustrated by root mean square deviation (RMSD), which captures motion over time (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), and RMSF of HVR-1 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: I438V A524T and ΔHVR-1 E2 were biophysically indistinguishable from one another but distinct from WT E2.
source: Here, I438V A524T and ΔHVR-1 E2 were biophysically indistinguishable from one another but distinct from WT E2.
evidence: This is shown by circular dichroism spectroscopy in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Estimation of the structural composition of I438V A524T and ΔHVR-1 E2 indicated a significant reduction of unordered components.
source: In particular, estimation of the structural composition of I438V A524T and ΔHVR-1 E2 indicated a significant reduction of unordered components Figure 4E; this is broadly consistent with our MD experiments.
evidence: This is shown by CD spectroscopy analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: DCC analysis of WT E2 suggests that motions within HVR-1 are transmitted throughout the protein.
source: DCC analysis of WT E2 suggests that motions within HVR-1 are transmitted throughout the protein (Figure 5B), consistent with an exerted force.
evidence: This is shown by dynamic cross-correlation analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: In the simulations of I438V A524T E2, HVR-1 is stabilised and correlated motions are absent.
source: In the simulations of I438V A524T E2, HVR-1 is stabilised (Figure 4) and these correlated motions are absent (Figure 5B), suggesting the lack of an entropic force.
evidence: This is shown by dynamic cross-correlation analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: ΔHVR-1 HCV exhibited a hyper-reactive phenotype above and beyond that of I438V A524T HCV.
source: In each case, ΔHVR-1 HCV exhibited a hyper-reactive phenotype above and beyond that of I438V A524T HCV; ΔHVR-1 HCV has very high infectious titres, low SR-B1 dependency, high instability and acute sensitivity to patient IgG.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple assays shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: S449P HCV was indistinguishable from I438V A524T HCV in every respect.
source: In every respect, S449P HCV was indistinguishable from I438V A524T HCV (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is shown by multiple assays in Figure 6A-D.

claim: MD simulations of S449P E2 demonstrated stabilisation of HVR-1 to the same extent as I438V A524T.
source: Moreover, MD simulations of S449P E2 demonstrated stabilisation of HVR-1 to the same extent as I438V A524T (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by MD simulations in Figure 6E-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The antibody selected culture exhibited low infectivity and high resistance to neutralisation.
source: The antibody selected culture exhibited low infectivity and high resistance to neutralisation, much like WT HCV.
evidence: This is shown by infectivity and neutralization assays in Figure 6G and H.

claim: The culture without antibody selection developed hallmarks of the hyper-reactive phenotype.
source: In contrast, the culture without selection developed hallmarks of the hyper-reactive phenotype; having increased infectivity and high sensitivity to neutralisation.
evidence: This is shown by infectivity and neutralization assays in Figure 6G and H.

claim: The culture without selection was dominated (>80%) by a triple E1E2 mutant: R317H, T387A, R408G.
source: NGS analysis of the culture with IgG selection revealed a mixed population of WT (>75%) and minor variants (<25% in total), suggesting limited adaptation, whereas the culture without selection was dominated (>80%) by a triple E1E2 mutant: R317H, T387A, R408G (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is shown by NGS analysis in Figure 6I.

claim: H77 L438V A524T E2 exhibits decreased HVR-1 dynamics when compared to WT H77.
source: Moreover, MD simulations indicate that H77 L438V A524T E2 exhibits decreased HVR-1 dynamics when compared to WT H77 (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is shown by MD simulations in Figure 6N.

claim: The HVR-1 safety-catch mechanism is conserved across diverse HCV genotypes.
source: These data are consistent with the HVR-1 safety-catch mechanism being conserved across diverse HCV genotypes.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments with H77 (genotype 1a) showing similar phenotypes to J6 (genotype 2a).

claim: HCV transmission continues at 1.5 million cases/year.
source: Therefore, understanding the conformational transitions and molecular triggers of E1E2 will reveal new biology and may guide HCV vaccinology; in the absence of a vaccine, HCV transmission continues at 1.5 million cases/year (as estimated by the World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: This is cited from WHO estimates.

claim: The glycoproteins of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), E1 and E2 (E1E2), do not possess the hallmarks of previously described fusion proteins.
source: However, the glycoproteins of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), E1 and E2 (E1E2), do not possess the hallmarks of previously described fusion proteins (El Omari et al., 2014; Flyak et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019), and may represent the prototype of a new class of fusion machinery.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: E1E2 may represent the prototype of a new class of fusion machinery.
source: However, the glycoproteins of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), E1 and E2 (E1E2), do not possess the hallmarks of previously described fusion proteins (El Omari et al., 2014; Flyak et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2014; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019), and may represent the prototype of a new class of fusion machinery.
evidence: This is speculation based on the unique features of E1E2.

claim: HVR-1 forms a disordered and dynamic protein tail.
source: The N-terminal hypervariable region-1 (HVR-1) of E2 binds SR-B1 and we recently demonstrated that HVR-1 forms a disordered and dynamic protein tail (Stejskal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors cited.

claim: HVR-1 binds SR-B1.
source: The N-terminal hypervariable region-1 (HVR-1) of E2 binds SR-B1 and we recently demonstrated that HVR-1 forms a disordered and dynamic protein tail (Stejskal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Antibody selection ensures that the safety catch mechanism remains engaged, maintaining low E1E2 reactivity and high resistance to nAbs.
source: Moreover, we provide evidence that antibody selection ensures that this safety catch mechanism remains engaged, maintaining low E1E2 reactivity and high resistance to nAbs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody selection experiments showing different evolutionary outcomes.

claim: Viral fusion proteins are broadly categorized as class-I, II, or III fusion machines.
source: Viral fusion proteins are broadly categorized as class-I, II, or III fusion machines, with diverse viruses within each class exhibiting similar mechanisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge in virology.

claim: HIV, Ebolavirus, and Coronaviruses all exhibit structurally similar class-I fusion machinery.
source: For example, HIV, Ebolavirus, and Coronaviruses all exhibit structurally similar class-I fusion machinery (Rey and Lok, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.
